T8A01: Single sideband (SSB) is a form of amplitude modulation: it's AM with the carrier and one sideband removed. This makes SSB much more efficient than standard AM.
T8A02: VHF packet radio commonly uses FM (or PM, phase modulation): the data tones are sent through an ordinary FM radio.
T8A03: SSB is used for long-distance weak-signal voice work on VHF/UHF, because it concentrates power into a narrow bandwidth and performs better than FM with weak signals.
T8A04: VHF and UHF voice repeaters commonly use FM (or PM). FM resists noise and works well for strong local signals.
T8A05: CW (Morse code) has the narrowest bandwidth of these, only about 150 Hz. SSB voice is about 3 kHz and FM about 10-15 kHz.
T8A06: By convention, upper sideband (USB) is used on 10 meters, VHF, and UHF (and on all HF bands 20 meters and higher). Lower sideband is used on 40, 80, and 160 meters.
T8A07: SSB uses a narrower bandwidth than FM (about 3 kHz vs 10-15 kHz). Narrow signals let more stations fit in a band and concentrate transmit power.
T8A08: A typical SSB voice signal is about 3 kHz wide, enough to carry intelligible speech frequencies.
T8A09: An FM voice signal on VHF repeaters is between 10 and 15 kHz wide.
T8A10: AM fast-scan TV (like old analog broadcast TV) is about 6 MHz wide. This is why it is only allowed on 70 cm and higher bands.
T8A11: A CW signal requires about 150 Hz of bandwidth, making it the narrowest common mode.
T8A12: FM has the 'capture effect': the receiver locks onto the strongest signal, so you can only receive one signal at a time. With SSB you can hear (and sometimes separate) overlapping signals.
T8B01: Satellite beacons transmit telemetry about the health and status of the satellite, such as battery voltages, temperatures, and solar panel current.
T8B02: Satellites share their transponder power among everyone using them. Excessive uplink power hogs that power and can block access by other users.
T8B03: Satellite tracking programs show real-time maps of the satellite's track, pass times with azimuth and elevation, and the Doppler-corrected frequency. All are provided.
T8B04: Amateur satellites use SSB, FM, and CW/data. Many FM satellites act like 'repeaters in the sky,' while linear transponder satellites relay SSB and CW.
T8B05: A satellite beacon is a transmission from the satellite that contains status (telemetry) information. It also helps you find the satellite's signal.
T8B06: Tracking programs use Keplerian elements, a set of numbers describing the satellite's orbit, to predict where the satellite will be.
T8B07: Doppler shift is the apparent change in frequency caused by relative motion. As a satellite approaches, its frequency appears higher; as it moves away, lower.
T8B08: In U/V mode, the uplink is UHF (70 cm) and the downlink is VHF (2 m). The first letter is the uplink band, the second the downlink.
T8B09: Spin fading is caused by the rotation of the satellite and its antennas, which changes the orientation of the signal relative to your antenna, causing periodic fading.
T8B10: LEO is Low Earth Orbit: satellites a few hundred km up that circle the Earth in about 100 minutes. Most amateur satellites, and the ISS, are in LEO.
T8B11: Anyone may receive telemetry from an amateur satellite. Amateur telemetry is not encrypted, and many listeners decode it.
T8B12: On a linear transponder satellite, adjust your uplink power so your signal on the downlink is about as strong as the satellite's beacon. Stronger than that means you're using too much power.
T8C01: Radio direction finding uses directional antennas and receivers to determine where a signal is coming from. It's used to locate noise sources and jammers.
T8C02: A hidden transmitter hunt (fox hunt) needs a directional antenna, such as a small Yagi, to determine the direction to the transmitter.
T8C03: Contesting is the activity of making as many contacts as possible during a specified period, often with an exchange of specific information.
T8C04: In a contest, send only the minimum information needed, such as call signs and the required exchange. Brevity lets everyone make more contacts. Always give your full call sign.
T8C05: A grid locator (Maidenhead grid square) is a letter-number designator for a geographic location, such as FN31. It's widely used on VHF/UHF and in digital modes.
T8C06: IRLP nodes are accessed over the air using DTMF (touch-tone) signals to connect to other nodes.
T8C07: VoIP (Voice Over Internet Protocol) delivers voice communications over the internet using digital techniques. Ham systems like EchoLink and IRLP use VoIP.
T8C08: IRLP (Internet Radio Linking Project) connects amateur radio systems, such as repeaters, via the internet, so a user on one repeater can talk through a distant one.
T8C09: EchoLink lets a licensed ham use a computer or smartphone app to connect via the internet to an EchoLink-enabled repeater or station and transmit through it, without using a radio.
T8C10: Before using EchoLink, you must register your call sign and provide proof of your license. This keeps unlicensed people from transmitting.
T8C11: A gateway is an amateur station that connects other amateur stations to the internet (for example, an EchoLink or Winlink gateway).
T8D01: Packet radio, IEEE 802.11 (Wi-Fi protocols adapted for ham mesh networks), and FT8 are all digital modes.
T8D02: FT8 is a digital mode designed to work with very weak signals (low signal-to-noise ratio), often below the level you can hear. It's very popular for making contacts on HF and 6 meters.
T8D03: APRS (Automatic Packet Reporting System) can transmit GPS position data, text messages, weather data, and more.
T8D04: NTSC is the analog fast-scan color TV standard used in North America (the old broadcast TV standard). Hams use it for amateur TV.
T8D05: APRS provides real-time tactical digital communications along with a map showing station locations. It's used in public service events and emergencies.
T8D06: PSK stands for Phase Shift Keying, a digital mode that encodes data by shifting the phase of the signal (as in PSK31).
T8D07: DMR (Digital Mobile Radio) uses time-division multiplexing to carry two digital voice signals (time slots) on a single 12.5 kHz channel.
T8D08: Packet radio transmissions include a header with the destination call sign, a checksum for error detection, and automatic repeat request (ARQ) when errors occur.
T8D09: CW (Continuous Wave) is another name for a Morse code transmission: the carrier is switched on and off to form dots and dashes.
T8D10: The WSJT-X software suite supports Earth-Moon-Earth (moonbounce), weak-signal propagation beacons (WSPR), and meteor scatter (MSK144), among other modes.
T8D11: ARQ (Automatic Repeat reQuest) is an error-correction method in which the receiving station detects errors and asks the sender to retransmit the bad data.
T8D12: An amateur radio mesh network (such as AREDN or Broadband-Hamnet) uses commercial Wi-Fi equipment with modified firmware to create a high-speed data network on amateur frequencies.
